extracted.intended_audience: law students, academics, patent practitioners, judges, and policymakers concerned with US patent eligibility for AI
extracted.subtask_description: Legal-analytic guidance on evaluating and drafting patents for AI inventions under US subject-matter-eligibility doctrine (Alice/Mayo framework), with policy recommendations for which kinds of AI inventions should be eligible. Focus is on Federal Circuit case law, USPTO MPEP guidance, and claim-drafting/evaluation implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentability requirements (§101–§103, utility/novelty/nonobviousness)
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent must be novel, nonobvious, useful, and meet subject-matter eligibility. The claims (defined by the specification) are examined against these statutory requirements (35 U.S.C. §§ 101–103, 112).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Novelty (§102): no single prior art reference discloses all claim elements. Nonobviousness (§103): invention not an obvious combination to a person of ordinary skill. Utility (§101 as use): must have a beneficial use. Subject-matter eligibility (§101) is a separate gate often dispositive for AI inventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstract-ideas/other judicial exceptions to §101
rubrics_metrics.description: Judge-made exceptions to §101 exclude laws of nature, physical phenomena, and abstract ideas from patentability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts treat certain mathematical formulas, fundamental economic practices, or mere data operations as abstract ideas; AI inventions often implicate the abstract-idea exception because they infer relationships from data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alice two-step test (Alice/Mayo framework)
rubrics_metrics.description: Step 1: Determine whether the claims are directed to a patent-ineligible concept (e.g., an abstract idea). Step 2: If so, determine whether additional claim elements contain an 'inventive concept' sufficient to transform the nature of the claim into a patent-eligible application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Token recitation of 'apply it' or generic computer components will not satisfy step two. Technical improvements that achieve something 'industry has not been able to obtain' can supply an inventive concept (Diehr example). Preemption risk is the driving concern of the test.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step-one inquiry — 'directed to' an abstract idea (centrality test)
rubrics_metrics.description: At step one, assess whether the claim is 'directed to' an abstract idea, which is more than merely 'contains' an idea; it asks how central the abstract idea is to the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lower courts must resolve how central a concept must be to be 'directed to' it. For software/AI, many claims are treated as directed to abstract ideas unless they are tied to an improvement in computer functioning or otherwise claim a specific technological solution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step-two inquiry — 'inventive concept' requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the claim's additional elements transform the ineligible concept into a patent-eligible application by providing an inventive concept beyond well-understood, routine, conventional activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An inventive concept often requires a technical solution to a technical problem (not merely automation or implementation on generic hardware). Mere use of conventional computer components or generic data operations fails; improvements in computer performance or new computer capabilities favor eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preemption as the animating concern
rubrics_metrics.description: The overarching policy concern in §101 analysis is preemption — whether a patent would unduly prevent others from using basic building blocks (ideas) and thus impede innovation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Findings should weigh whether the claim would 'totally preempt' all applications of the idea; claims that leave alternative ways to achieve the same result are less problematic. Total preemption is a strong indicator of ineligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bandai (McRO) framework for software/AI eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Federal Circuit in McRO, Inc. v. Bandai Namco identified factors supporting eligibility for computer-implemented inventions: (1) an improvement to computer capabilities; (2) automation carried out in a way different from the human-performed prior art; and (3) absence of total preemption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply Bandai to AI: claims that give machines new capabilities (not mere automation of human thought processes), that operate in a qualitatively different manner than manual methods, and that avoid preempting all such automation, are more likely eligible. Bandai is proposed as a preferable rubric for AI eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical-solution-to-technical-problem criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims are more likely to supply an inventive concept if they represent a technical solution to a technical problem (i.e., they improve the functioning of the computer or solve a computer-specific problem).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diehr-like examples (improving a physical or computational process) show eligibility; courts should favor technological improvements over abstract results or mere data manipulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conventional or routine data operations do not supply eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Adding conventional data-collection, storage, or generic algorithmic steps to an abstract idea is insufficient to transform the claim into an eligible invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: claiming 'using machine learning' broadly or reciting common ML techniques (regression, decision trees) without claiming a specific technical improvement will likely fail Alice step two.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims merely automating mental processes are suspect
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that merely automate tasks that could be performed mentally by humans (i.e., mental processes) risk being directed to abstract ideas and thus ineligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: However, automation can be eligible if the automated process is qualitatively different from the manual prior art and confers new computer capabilities (per Bandai).

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim breadth and specificity (avoid overbroad claims)
rubrics_metrics.description: Excessively broad claims that preempt a wide swath of techniques (e.g., all machine learning methods for a purpose) are more likely to be ineligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft claims to describe particular AI processes, architectures, training steps, or technical improvements to avoid preemption; narrow, particularized claim language reduces risk of being categorized as an abstract idea or an 'application' that preempts the field.

rubrics_metrics.name: USPTO MPEP guidance (2014 vs 2019/2022) and 'step zero' streamlined analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO's MPEP revisions (notably 2019) introduced examiner guidance including a 'streamlined analysis at step zero,' a 'second prong of step one,' and efforts to circumscribe what constitutes an abstract idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical effect: increased allowance rates for AI patents post-2019. But the Comment cautions that the USPTO lacks authority to make substantive law and its guidance may be inconsistent with Federal Circuit precedent; applicants should favor binding case law when assessing eligibility risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Circumscribing 'abstract ideas' — USPTO examples and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO attempted to narrow what counts as an abstract idea via examples (e.g., an 'eligible neural network' example) and guidance that certain specific improvements are not abstract.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: District courts may reject the USPTO's examples if inconsistent with case law; reliance on USPTO examples does not guarantee judicial deference. Examiners' inconsistent application of examples creates applicant uncertainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Datasets vs models vs applications — policy distinctions
rubrics_metrics.description: Normative recommendations: datasets should be patent ineligible because they stymie follow-on innovation; applications of AI (application-in-context claims) should generally be ineligible; AI methods and models should usually be patent eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy-based rubric: allow patents that incentivize development of AI methods/models without chilling follow-on research; exclude patents whose primary effect is to preempt raw data or broad applications that block others from using AI in particular contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weight and authority of USPTO guidance vs judicial precedent
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO's guidance is influential for examination but is not entitled to deference in courts and cannot create substantive law; Federal Circuit and Supreme Court precedents control eligibility outcomes in litigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants and counsel should evaluate eligibility risk against binding case law (Alice, Mayo, Diehr, Bandai, Benson, Flook) rather than rely solely on MPEP examples or examiner statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tangible-result test is not dispositive
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts should not treat production of a 'tangible result' as a necessary condition for eligibility; Bandai was eligible even though it did not produce a tangible physical product.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid relying on 'tangible result' as a safe harbor; focus instead on whether claim yields a technical improvement or new machine capability without undue preemption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid claiming generic 'machine learning' without inventive detail
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that recite machine learning generically (e.g., 'using machine learning to optimize X') are likely to be treated as abstract ideas or routine data operations and thus ineligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Better practice: claim particular training regimens, model architectures, data transformations, loss functions, iterative steps, or computational resource improvements that show a concrete technical innovation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish human-performed prior art from claimed automated process
rubrics_metrics.description: Eligibility is supported when the claimed automation carries out tasks differently from how humans perform them (qualitatively different process), not merely by automating the same mental steps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrate in the specification how the AI method changes the order, type, or nature of steps compared to the human technique and how this yields a new computer capability or technical benefit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be mindful of litigation risk and examiner inconsistency
rubrics_metrics.description: Because guidance has changed and courts remain the ultimate arbiter, many patents granted under permissive MPEP guidance may face invalidation. Examiners may apply guidance inconsistently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants should prepare for potential litigation by grounding claims in technical detail, evidencing technological improvements, and anticipating Alice/Mayo challenges in prosecution and claim drafting.
